mcqs.question: A team's `domain/invoice.ts` imports `fetchJson` from `../infrastructure/http` and `trackEvent` from `../infrastructure/analytics`, and the same function decides that an invoice with no lines is invalid. Which diagnosis matches the dependency rule that makes layering pay off?
options: Nothing structural: a domain module may call infrastructure directly when the calls are short and the rule stays easy to read.
It fuses a use case with a rule and imports outward; the rule belongs in pure domain code and an application use case should orchestrate through a gateway.
The folder structure is wrong: the codebase needs presentation, application, domain, and infrastructure folders before the rule can be separated from transport.
The technology mix is wrong: domain code should use a different HTTP library from the UI, so the two layers cannot share technical choices.
mcqs.explanation: Layering is a dependency rule, not a folder vocabulary: inner layers own the rules and must not import outward, so a rule can be exercised without network, analytics, or a DOM, and swapping an adapter never reaches into business code. Here the function both orchestrates I/O and states the rule, and its imports point outward into infrastructure, so the arrow is inverted; the fix is a pure domain rule plus an application use case that receives a gateway and lets the composition root choose the adapter. The strongest distractor is the folder split: moving the file under `domain/` changes no import, so it still imports `../infrastructure/http`, and the coupling, the test cost, and the migration cost are identical. 'Short calls are fine' confuses the size of the call with the direction of the dependency, and 'a different HTTP library per layer' mistakes technology variety for separation.

mcqs.question: A team organizes the frontend by features. Which practice actually preserves the benefit of that organization?
options: A global components/, hooks/, and utils/ tree kept alongside the features, so shared code has one home.
A small public API per feature plus enforced import rules, so no feature reaches into another feature's internals.
Free cross-folder imports between features, since everything lives in the same repository anyway.
Forcing every helper, however tiny, into a feature folder so that nothing is ever shared.
mcqs.explanation: Feature organization works when each feature exposes a small public API and import rules prevent reaching into another feature's internals, with genuinely shared code in an explicit shared area. The strongest distractor (the global tree) fails because it recreates the exact coupling feature organization exists to avoid: unrelated code becomes coupled in components, hooks, and utils folders, and ownership and deletion get harder. The last distractor overcorrects: stable primitives and cross-cutting infrastructure can remain shared.

mcqs.question: A team signs off a user flow after testing it against `vite dev`. CI then runs `vite build` and deploys the output. Which check supports the claim that the flow works in the deployed artifact?
options: Run the same flow against the built output, locally or in the deployment; `vite dev` and `vite build` are different pipelines, not one pipeline plus minification.
Testing it against `vite dev`, because dev and build share the module graph and differ only in minification and asset hashing.
Testing it against `vite dev --mode production`, because the mode flag switches the dev server to the production pipeline.
Nothing further: a green `vite build` is enough, because a successful build proves every code path executes.
mcqs.explanation: Vite has two pipelines: the dev server serves native ESM and pre-bundles dependencies on demand, while the production build emits a separate bundle with its own target, entries, splitting, and asset handling (https://vite.dev/guide/build); only exercising the built artifact covers the code that ships. The strongest distractor is the 'only minification differs' claim: the build also replaces `import.meta.env`, applies the build target, tree-shakes, rewrites asset URLs, and resolves modules differently, so a dev-only assumption can pass review and fail after deploy. `--mode production` only changes which `.env` files load and the value of `import.meta.env.MODE` (https://vite.dev/guide/env-and-mode), and a green build proves compilation, not runtime behaviour such as a missing env value or a broken asset path.

mcqs.question: Why should a workspace package expose deliberate entry points through package.json exports?
options: So every internal file becomes importable from outside, giving consumers maximum flexibility.
Because a barrel file that re-exports everything is the recommended default entry point.
So consumers depend on supported names and contracts rather than the directory layout, letting internal refactors stay internal.
Because exports only matter for packages published to a registry, not for internal workspace packages.
mcqs.explanation: A public entry point is a boundary you can evolve deliberately: consumers depend on supported names and contracts, and the exports field can enumerate entry points while avoiding exposing implementation files (https://nodejs.org/api/packages.html#exports). The strongest distractor (the barrel default) fails because Turborepo's guidance notes barrel files can be difficult for compilers and bundlers and recommends explicit exports (https://turbo.build/repo/docs/crafting-your-repository/structuring-a-repository). The last distractor fails because boundaries matter inside the workspace too: deep imports turn internal refactors into repository-wide edits.

mcqs.question: A pnpm workspace package declares @acme/ui as workspace:*, but no local package matches at install time. What happens?
options: pnpm silently installs the best-matching @acme/ui from the registry so the build keeps moving.
pnpm creates a placeholder stub and prints a warning to address later.
pnpm rewrites the dependency to a plain semver range and retries the registry automatically.
Installation fails, because workspace: resolves only to a matching local workspace package.
mcqs.explanation: The workspace: protocol tells pnpm to resolve only to a matching local workspace package; if the requested local version is absent, installation fails, which exposes accidental version drift early and keeps local development and CI deterministic (https://pnpm.io/workspaces). The strongest distractor (silent registry fallback) describes exactly the failure mode the protocol was designed to prevent, and it is what would happen with a plain version spec.

mcqs.question: A Turborepo build task sets inputs to ["src/**"], but the build also reads vite.config.ts and the DEPLOY_ENV variable. What is the risk?
options: Cache hits can restore stale artifacts, because output-affecting inputs are missing from the hash.
No risk: Turborepo automatically discovers every config file and environment variable a task reads.
The task fails immediately with a missing-cache-input error, so the mistake is self-detecting.
Only the dev server is affected; production builds bypass the task cache entirely.
mcqs.explanation: A cache is only safe when all output-affecting inputs, including relevant environment values and configuration, are represented in the hash; Turborepo hashes inputs to decide whether to restore results and assumes tasks are deterministic (https://turbo.build/repo/docs/crafting-your-repository/caching). Specifying inputs also opts out of the default behavior of hashing all source-controlled files in the package (https://turbo.build/repo/docs/crafting-your-repository/configuring-tasks). The strongest distractor (auto-discovery) fails because Turborepo hashes exactly what is declared: an undeclared env var is invisible to the fingerprint and nothing errors.

mcqs.question: In Nx, app A depends on lib L (a project-graph edge). What does that imply when running tests?
options: A's test automatically waits for L's test, because every project edge implies the same-named target dependency.
L's test waits for A's test, since dependents are validated before their dependencies.
Nothing automatic: A's test does not wait for L's test unless a task dependency such as ^test is configured.
Nx refuses to run both tests in one invocation and requires two separate commands.
mcqs.explanation: The project graph describes projects and their source or dependency relationships, while the task graph describes concrete targets and the task-to-task dependencies needed for one invocation; two projects can depend on a library while their test tasks run independently unless a ^test relationship is configured (https://nx.dev/concepts/mental-model). The strongest distractor fails because it mirrors the project graph onto the task graph, serializing work that has no ordering requirement and conflating architecture with scheduling.

mcqs.question: A Vite app gates verbose logging with: if (import.meta.env.VITE_DEBUG). The env file sets VITE_DEBUG=false in production. What happens?
options: Verbose logging turns on: the value is the string "false", which is truthy.
The gate works, because Vite coerces "false" to boolean false at build time.
The build fails with a type error for using a string where a boolean is expected.
The variable is undefined in production, because VITE_ variables are only defined in development.
mcqs.explanation: Vite exposes VITE_-prefixed variables through import.meta.env as strings, so they must be parsed into booleans, numbers, and URLs at a typed configuration boundary (https://vite.dev/guide/env-and-mode). The strongest distractor (automatic coercion) fails because no coercion happens; the same root cause breaks strict comparisons too, since 'true' === true is false. The last distractor misreads modes: files like .env.production exist precisely to define values for production builds.

mcqs.question: Three teams ship one React SPA as a single artifact, and every release needs a coordinated freeze because any change lands in the same bundle. They share a router, an auth flow, and a design system. What would justify splitting it into micro-frontends?
options: Slower builds: each team's build time has grown, so splitting the repository restores fast feedback for everyone.
Independent delivery: each team needs to deploy its area on its own cadence, so release coordination itself is the bottleneck.
Framework freedom: each team wants its own framework, and multiple frameworks are the main benefit of splitting.
Team count: three teams work on the frontend, so there should be three deployables, one per team.
mcqs.explanation: Micro-frontends buy independent build and deploy inside one browser runtime; they pay off when that independence solves a real organisational or migration problem, and they cost explicit rules for DOM ownership, routing, authentication, shared dependencies, observability, and failure handling, because the page is still one runtime (https://single-spa.js.org/docs/microfrontends-concept/). The strongest distractor is the team-count inference, because it is the usual justification: several teams can ship independently inside one deployable with trunk-based work, feature flags, and a release train, so headcount alone buys the runtime cost without the benefit. Slow builds are a task-graph and caching problem, not a runtime-decomposition problem; multiple frameworks mainly make sense during a migration, and outside it they multiply bundle and operational cost, which is why the single-spa guidance recommends one framework.

mcqs.question: Host and remote both declare React in Module Federation's shared config. Why might the page still end up with two React copies?
options: Share scopes choose a copy based on version requirements and singleton settings; incompatible ranges or a missing singleton policy can load multiple copies.
Federation always dedupes shared dependencies automatically, so two copies are impossible.
React cannot be listed in shared at all; each build must bundle it privately.
Duplicate output.uniqueName values always duplicate every shared dependency.
mcqs.explanation: Shared dependencies are registered in a share scope rather than necessarily bundled privately, and version requirements and singleton settings influence which shared copy is consumed, so stateful libraries like React need an intentional compatibility policy (https://webpack.js.org/concepts/module-federation/). The strongest distractor (automatic dedupe) fails because sharing is negotiated at runtime, not guaranteed. The uniqueName distractor confuses two documented failure modes: duplicate output.uniqueName values collide on the runtime name, they do not control share-scope version selection.

mcqs.question: One frontend artifact must be promoted unchanged through dev, staging, and production with different API URLs. What is the sound design?
options: Build a separate artifact per environment using .env.staging and .env.production, which keeps each build simple.
Keep everything in import.meta.env and treat it as a runtime configuration service the app reads after deploy.
Typed, validated build-time public values plus environment-specific non-secret values injected at deployment or request time and schema-validated before bootstrap.
Encrypt the secrets into the bundle and decrypt them in the browser at runtime, so only the app can read them.
mcqs.explanation: Build-time values are immutable once bundled, so a single promoted artifact needs non-secret runtime configuration injected from a controlled server response, HTML bootstrap, or equivalent deployment mechanism, with its schema validated before bootstrapping (https://vite.dev/guide/env-and-mode). The strongest distractor (per-environment builds) fails because mode-specific env files are selected at build time, producing different artifacts, which is exactly what promotion forbids. The encryption distractor fails because a browser can inspect every value it receives; encryption the client can undo is not secrecy.

mcqs.question: A PR to `@acme/ui` removes the deprecated `variant="ghost"` prop, adds an optional `loading` prop, and fixes a hover-state CSS bug. Every consumer inside the workspace already stopped passing `ghost`. Under semantic versioning of the package's public API, what bump does the release require?
options: Minor: one prop left and one arrived, so the API change nets out to a compatible modification.
Patch: the user-visible result is a CSS fix plus removal of dead code that no consumer passes anymore.
Major: deleting a public prop is a breaking API change, and in-workspace usage does not shrink the published contract.
Minor: the removed prop was already deprecated, so deleting it only completes an announced change.
mcqs.explanation: Semver describes compatibility of the public API between released versions: removing an export, prop, or accepted value breaks code written against 2.x, so it is major, while a compatible addition like `loading` alone would be minor and a compatible fix alone would be patch (https://semver.org/#semantic-versioning-specification-semver, item 8). Version from the package's public API, not from what this repository happens to import today: external consumers and old lockfiles still call `ghost`, and in-repo adoption is evidence for shipping a codemod, not for a smaller bump. The strongest distractor is the deprecation one: deprecation is a migration signal that the surface is still present, so removing it changes what 2.x promised — the announced notice shortens the migration window, it does not make the deletion compatible. The net-change option fails because compatibility is conjunctive: one compatible addition cannot offset one incompatible removal, and the patch option confuses the visible outcome with the API contract.

mcqs.question: A workspace tags every project and runs `@nx/enforce-module-boundaries` as an error on every pull request. Which violation can still merge green?
options: A `scope:client` library importing `scope:admin` code through a relative path, because the rule only inspects bare package specifiers.
A `scope:client` library importing a file deep inside another `scope:client` library, because the constraint allows same-scope edges and entry-point granularity is a separate mechanism.
A library importing a package it never declared in its own `package.json`, because the rule only reads source imports.
A brand-new library created without tags, because untagged projects are treated as compatible with every other project.
mcqs.explanation: Module boundaries answer "which project may depend on which", so a same-scope edge stays legal by design; which file a consumer may reach inside that project is the public entry point, enforced by `package.json` `exports` (the two mechanisms complement each other). The strongest distractor is the relative-path one, because filesystem escapes feel invisible to linting — but the Nx rule checks TypeScript imports (relative and package specifiers) and declared `package.json` dependencies during linting, so crossing `scope:client` into `scope:admin` is reported either way (https://nx.dev/docs/features/enforce-module-boundaries). The undeclared-dependency option fails for the same reason: declared versus imported dependencies are part of what the rule verifies. The untagged option inverts documented behaviour — projects without tags cannot depend on any other project, so that mistake fails loudly instead of shipping.

mcqs.question: A web app and a native app share one general-purpose orders service. The web app needs a composed dashboard (three calls reshaped into a view model) plus its own pagination and caching; the native app is fine calling the raw endpoints. The team adds a BFF for the web app. Where does each responsibility belong?
options: Neither: a BFF should forward requests unchanged so the shared service remains the only place with behaviour.
Both in the BFF: the shared service stays generic, and each client implements the rules its own interface needs.
Aggregation in the BFF, and a copy of the tenant rule in the BFF too, to save a round trip on every dashboard load.
Aggregation and view-model shaping in the BFF; the rule "a user may only read orders of their own tenant" in the domain service, so every client and future entry point inherits it.
mcqs.explanation: A BFF is justified by materially different data, performance, or release needs, and its job is client-specific orchestration: aggregation, mapping, response shaping, pagination and caching tuned to one UI. Business rules stay in domain services, while cross-cutting authorization and monitoring belong in the gateway or platform layer (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/backends-for-frontends). The strongest distractor is the one that moves the tenant rule into the BFF, because a security rule implemented at one client's edge protects exactly that edge: the native client by design calls the raw endpoints, every future client would have to reimplement the check, and the two copies drift until one of them is wrong. The forward-everything option describes a proxy, which adds a deploy, a security surface, and a network hop without shaping anything — the bank's own rule is that a BFF which only forwards should be deleted.

mcqs.question: `apps/web` imports `packages/ui`; `turbo.json` orders `web:build` after `ui:build`, and `tsc --noEmit` at the root type-checks the whole workspace as one program, slowly. What does adding `references: [{ "path": "../../packages/ui" }]` to `apps/web/tsconfig.json` actually change?
options: The bundler now resolves `@acme/ui` to the local source and guarantees the shipped bundle contains the latest `ui` code.
It replaces the `dependsOn: ["^build"]` edge, so the task runner no longer has to order those builds.

`tsc -b` can build `packages/ui` first and let `apps/web` consume its declaration output, making the type build incremental per project — it changes nothing about runtime resolution or about which files consumers may import.
Without it TypeScript refuses to type-check any import that crosses a workspace package boundary.
mcqs.explanation: A reference declares a compiler-project edge: imports from a referenced project load its `.d.ts` output, and `tsc --build` finds references, detects up-to-date projects, and builds the out-of-date ones in dependency order (https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/project-references.html). It is a type-build decision — the referenced project needs `composite: true` and declarations — and it says nothing about how the bundler resolves a specifier or which files a consumer may import; `exports` and the bundler still own that. The strongest distractor is the one that deletes `dependsOn: ["^build"]`: the task runner schedules every package task (build, test, lint, assets) against its own graph, while references only express the TypeScript compiler graph, so removing the ordering edge brings back builds against stale or missing artifacts (https://nx.dev/concepts/mental-model). The bundler-resolution option confuses module resolution with the compiler graph, and the last option is simply false: `paths` or workspace links type-check across packages today, just without per-project incrementality.

scenarios.prompt: This Vite app cannot turn debug logging off in production, and a security review flagged the config module. Find every defect and rewrite the configuration boundary.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Walkthrough: (1) The debug gate is broken because env values are strings: import.meta.env.VITE_DEBUG is the string 'false', which is truthy, so verbose logging is enabled in production. The same root cause would break a === true check, since 'true' === true is false. (2) The payments secret is a leak: Vite bundles VITE_-prefixed variables into client code at build time, so anything prefixed VITE_ is public configuration and must never contain secrets. The charge call must go through a backend or serverless function that holds the secret server-side; the client only sends the card token to our own endpoint. (3) apiUrl is an unparsed string: parse it with new URL(...) at the boundary so a malformed value fails at startup or build time, not at the first fetch. (4) Nothing is validated: required public values should be validated at startup or build time so a missing VITE_API_URL fails loudly instead of producing undefined URLs. Rewrite: a single config module that reads import.meta.env once, parses and validates, and exports a typed object; the rest of the app imports typed config, never import.meta.env. Sketch: const raw = { apiUrl: import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL, debug: import.meta.env.VITE_DEBUG }; if (!raw.apiUrl) throw new Error('VITE_API_URL is required'); export const config = { apiUrl: new URL(raw.apiUrl), debug: raw.debug === 'true' };. Operationally, remember that shell variables have higher priority than .env files and that the dev server must be restarted after changing env files.
rubric: Identifies the string-truthiness bug: 'false' is a truthy string, so debug logging is on in production, and no automatic coercion exists.
Identifies the secret leak: VITE_ values are bundled into the client at build time, so the payments secret must move to a backend or serverless function.
Parses and validates at one typed boundary: URL construction, boolean parsing, and required-value checks instead of scattering raw strings.
States the operational facts: values are strings, shell variables override .env files, and the dev server needs a restart after env changes.
Keeps the fix at a single seam so application code imports a typed config module rather than import.meta.env directly.

scenarios.prompt: CI builds this monorepo. A PR whose only change was `apps/web/vite.config.ts` got a cache hit for the `apps/web` build task, and the staging deployment kept serving the previous API host. The build script is `vite build`; `vite.config.ts` maps `process.env.DEPLOY_ENV` to the API base URL baked into the bundle, and CI exports `DEPLOY_ENV=staging` on the staging pipeline. Diagnose the caching failure and fix the task definition.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
**Diagnosis.** The cache is behaving as designed against an incomplete fingerprint. `inputs` replaces the package's default input set, so `apps/web/vite.config.ts` is no longer hashed, and `DEPLOY_ENV` is read by the config at build time and inlined through `define`, but it is not declared in `env`, so its value never enters the hash. The PR changed only the config, so the computed hash matched an earlier build and Turborepo restored that artifact: a correct hit on the wrong inputs. `outputs: ["dist/**"]` did the rest, restoring the old bundle exactly as configured.

**Fix.** In the root `turbo.json`: `inputs: ["src/**", "vite.config.ts"]` and `env: ["DEPLOY_ENV"]`, keeping `outputs: ["dist/**"]` and `dependsOn: ["^build"]`. `["$TURBO_DEFAULT$", "!README.md"]` is the alternative when you want the default package-file set minus files proven irrelevant. If several tasks hash `DEPLOY_ENV`, use `globalEnv` instead of repeating `env`; `passThroughEnv` alone makes the value available but does not affect the hash, and `globalDependencies` takes file globs (for example a root `tsconfig.json`), not environment variables. `package.json`, `turbo.json`, and the lockfile are always inputs, so only project-owned files like `vite.config.ts` need adding.

**Verification.** `turbo run build --dry=json` (or `--summarize`) shows what is actually hashed; changing `DEPLOY_ENV` must produce a miss, and a clean rebuild must equal the restored artifact. The governing rule: every output-affecting input must be in the hash, a hit only proves the hashed inputs matched, and Turborepo assumes the task is deterministic (https://turborepo.com/docs/crafting-your-repository/caching, https://turborepo.com/docs/reference/configuration).
rubric: Reads the hit as an incomplete fingerprint — config file and env value missing from the hash — rather than a broken or forced cache.
Knows that declaring `inputs` replaces the default package-file set, which is how `vite.config.ts` left the hash.
Repairs both gaps: the config in `inputs` (or `$TURBO_DEFAULT$`), `DEPLOY_ENV` in `env` or `globalEnv`, and `outputs` kept; separates `env`, `passThroughEnv`, and `globalDependencies`.
Verifies with a dry run or run summary plus a deliberate env change that must miss, instead of trusting the edit.
States the determinism rule: a cache hit is not evidence of correctness.

scenarios.prompt: Refactor this workspace UI package so consumers can only use a deliberate public API. Explain what breaks, why it breaks, and why the change is worth it.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
**Diagnosis.** (1) `main` and `types` describe only the root entry; with no `exports` map, Node and bundlers fall back to filesystem resolution inside the package, so `@acme/ui/dist/internal/button` resolves today. That is not a contract: renaming `dist/internal/` or changing the build layout breaks the consumer with no version bump and no deprecation signal. (2) The barrel re-exports `internal/merge-styles`, so an implementation helper is public API by accident and every internal name becomes something to version. (3) Nothing enumerates the surface, so the package has no place to declare what it supports.

**Refactor.** Add an `exports` map that lists only supported entry points: `{ ".": { "types": "./dist/index.d.ts", "default": "./dist/index.js" } }`, with `import`/`require` conditions if the package ships both formats. With only `.` listed, `@acme/ui/dist/internal/button` stops resolving (`ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED` in Node, a resolution error in bundlers that honour the field); add `./button` or `./styles` only as deliberate decisions, never to keep old imports alive. Remove `export * from './internal/merge-styles'` from `src/index.ts` and decide explicitly whether `mergeStyles` is public: either promote it behind a named entry with docs and tests, or keep it internal, inline it in `Button`, expose a supported `className`/`style` API, and delete the marketing import. Migrate `apps/marketing/src/hero.tsx` in the same change so the build stays green.

**What breaks, and why that is the point.** The deep import and the root import of `mergeStyles` are the two accidental dependencies; each break is a consumer that relied on layout rather than contract, and migrating them is the refactor.

**Guard.** Add a test that imports only public entries and asserts the exported surface, plus a resolution check through the bundler. TypeScript with an older `moduleResolution` (`node10`) ignores `exports` and can still type-check the deep import that fails at runtime, so the guard must exercise resolution/build, not only `tsc`.

**Payoff.** Consumers depend on names you can version, internal refactors stop being repository-wide edits, ownership and API review become explicit, and compilers and bundlers stop paying for a barrel that re-exports everything (https://nodejs.org/api/packages.html#package-entry-points, https://turbo.build/repo/docs/crafting-your-repository/structuring-a-repository).
rubric: Identifies the missing `exports` map as the reason subpaths (including `dist/internal/*`) are reachable, even though `main` and `types` name only the root entry.
Removes the internal export from the barrel and makes an explicit promote-or-privatise decision for `mergeStyles`, migrating the consumer in the same change.
Writes an `exports` map with `types`/`default` and states which imports break after it (`dist/internal/button`, the root `mergeStyles` import) and how each is migrated.
Accounts for tooling: Node and bundlers enforce `exports`, while an older TS `moduleResolution` may still type-check deep imports, so the guard must exercise resolution.
Adds a CI or public-surface check so an accidental export fails review instead of relying on documentation.

scenarios.prompt: This shell mounts two federated remotes. Each remote works alone in its own dev server, but mounted together one remote's React hooks throw and the console shows a shared-scope version warning. Diagnose every defect against Module Federation's documented mechanics, then list the organizational policies that are missing.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
**Start from the symptom.** A hook error plus a shared-scope version warning is the signature of two React runtimes on the page. Sibling remotes are handed the same share scope by the common host, so this is a policy problem, not a loading problem.

**(1) Asymmetric React policy — the cause of the hook error.** `remote_one` declares `requiredVersion: '^18.2.0'` with `singleton: true`; `remote_two` declares `^18.0.0` and no `singleton`. In a share scope a consumer takes the highest registered version that satisfies its range, and a build that is not a singleton consumer may fall back to its own bundled copy. When the provided React does not satisfy one of those ranges, the singleton side is forced onto the provided copy while the non-singleton side keeps its own: one remote runs on the host's React and the other on its own, and hooks throw with an invalid hook call. That asymmetry is exactly why one remote breaks and not both, and why each works alone. The warning names the module and the range that went unsatisfied; fix the policy, not the warning. Use one shared policy for `react` and `react-dom` across host and remotes (same supported major, aligned `requiredVersion`, `singleton: true`), defined once in a shared config package instead of copy-pasted. A shared module that is already loaded is not replaced, so the host must settle the policy before its entry consumes React.

**(2) Duplicate container name — a separate defect with a different signature.** `remote_two` still declares `name: 'remote_one'`. The container name is the global a consumer reads, so the second `remoteEntry.js` registers over the first remote's global; a host resolving `remote_two` by name gets a container that does not exist under that name. `output.uniqueName` must also differ per build (webpack derives it from the package name): two builds sharing it share the chunk-loading global and become indistinguishable to the shared-module runtime, which uses the unique name to break ties between identical versions. Fix both explicitly and review them as config invariants; expect this to surface as a container or module-resolution error, or as one remote clobbering the other, not as the hook error.

**(3) The static imports are not the defect.** With the remotes declared in the host's `remotes` config, webpack injects the remote entry script, waits for the global, calls `init(scope)`, and obtains modules through `get()`; `import Catalog from 'remote_one/Catalog'` is the supported form and the asynchronous chunk loading happens underneath it. The documented async-boundary fix (`import('./bootstrap')`) belongs to the other error, "Shared module is not available for eager consumption", which appears when the entry itself consumes a shared module before the scope exists; adding the boundary is cheap insurance, and `eager: true` should be limited to the host (https://webpack.js.org/concepts/module-federation/).

**Missing policies.** Versioned remote URLs with deliberate pinning or selection; defined behaviour when a remote entry or an exposed module fails to load (fallback, skip, error boundary); observability of load, init, and render failures by remote and version; ownership of shared libraries; contract tests for each remote's exposed API; release, rollback, and security review in the remote's pipeline.
rubric: Attributes the hook error and the version warning to the asymmetric React share policy (divergent `requiredVersion`, missing `singleton`), not to the import syntax.
Explains that a configured remote's static import is served by webpack's script/init/get handshake, and reserves the async-boundary fix for eager consumption of shared modules in the entry.
Treats the duplicate container name as an independent defect with its own failure signature, and requires a unique `name` plus a unique `output.uniqueName` per build.
Proposes one shared-dependency policy owned centrally (aligned range, singleton, single source of config) and a way to verify the scope at runtime.
Adds runtime policies: versioned remote URLs, failure/fallback behaviour, and observability by remote and version.

scenarios.prompt: Boundary lint is green on every pull request in this workspace, yet a client dashboard shipped while importing admin internals and reaching into another package's private files. Explain every reason the enforcement let it through, then rewrite the configuration so the same pull request fails.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
Start from the mechanism, not the tags: the tags and constraints below are correct, and they are not the reason this merged.

(1) The rule never ran on the violating file. `files: ['apps/**/*.ts']` matches neither `.tsx` nor anything under `libs/`, and the offending import lives in `libs/client/dashboard/src/Dashboard.tsx`. In ESLint flat config a rule configured under `files` applies only to files matching that glob, so boundary violations in `.tsx` components and in every library file are outside the linter's reach. This is the primary defect: a rule that is not applied cannot fail.

(2) CI narrowed it twice. `"lint": "eslint \"apps/**\""` runs ESLint over `apps/` only, so even a corrected `files` glob would be filtered back down by the invocation. Coverage has to be fixed in both places — the config and the command — or CI keeps linting a subset of the workspace.

(3) One violation is a filesystem escape: `../../../admin/src/lib/tenant-filter` crosses `scope:client` -> `scope:admin` by relative path and bypasses `package.json` entirely. Two consequences, not one: the boundary rule (once it runs) reports the tag violation, and separately the project graph never sees the edge, so the task runner cannot order admin's build before client's (`dependsOn: ["^build"]` follows declared dependencies) and a cache hit can ship client code built against a stale admin. The fix is not a wider constraint: the dependency is wrong, so call the admin service through its public API or move the shared helper to `scope:shared`.

(4) The other violation is legal by design. `@acme/ui/src/internal/merge-styles` goes from `scope:client` to `scope:shared`, which `depConstraints` permits, so no amount of tag fixing flags it. `depConstraints` governs direction between projects; which file inside a project is reachable is an entry-point contract, and with `main` and no `exports` map every file under `packages/ui` is reachable. Add an `exports` map that enumerates the real entry points (`"."`, and `"./format"` only if consumers need it) so the deep subpath fails at resolution, and remove `merge-styles` from the public surface or promote it deliberately.

Rewrite: `files: ['**/*.{ts,tsx,js,jsx}']` with the same `depConstraints`; CI runs `eslint .` (or lint per project over the whole workspace); `@acme/ui` gets an `exports` map plus a small test that imports the public entries and asserts a deep subpath throws; the relative cross-project import is replaced by the public entry; new projects get their tags from the generator/template so nothing lands untagged.

Prove it instead of asserting it: add one allowed edge and one forbidden edge as fixtures (or a throwaway branch) and confirm lint fails on the forbidden one in CI. A boundary rule nobody has seen fail is a hypothesis, and this pull request is what a hypothesis costs.
rubric: Identifies the coverage gap first — the `files` glob excludes `.tsx` and `libs/`, and the CI command re-narrows it — instead of blaming missing tags.
Separates graph direction (`depConstraints`, tag-to-tag edges) from entry-point surface (`package.json` `exports`), and explains why the same-scope deep import is legal under the current constraints.
Treats the relative `../../../admin/...` import as an invisible edge with build/cache consequences, and fixes the dependency rather than widening the allowed tags.
Proposes an executable proof that a forbidden edge now fails (negative fixture, canary branch), not just a corrected config.
Keeps the fix in versioned config and CI so it survives contributor turnover, rather than relying on review or documentation.
